meta.title: "You always do this" — why your child believes in overgeneralisations | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child not to accept "always/never" as truth and not to let words define who they are. Game-based course for children aged 8–12.

hero.headline: "You always do this!" — and your child already believes it?
hero.subheadline: "Always", "never", "every time" — it sounds like a fact. But one exception is enough to make the whole claim fall apart. Your child doesn't notice.

media.alt: A child being labelled through the word 'always'

pain.title: "You always" — that's not a description, it's pressure
pain.body:
"You're always late", "you always mess everything up", "it's always like this with you". At school, at home, among friends. The child knows this isn't always true — but starts to doubt and explain themselves instead of checking.

This isn't exaggerating or lying on purpose. Words like "always", "never", "everyone" sound like facts — and the brain takes them seriously. But a single exception is enough to make the claim fall apart. When a child lacks the skill to notice this, they accept the label and go on the defensive instead of thinking.

The result — they believe the exaggeration and build a false picture of themselves. "I always do this", "maybe that really is me" — and the label becomes part of how they see themselves.
